title: Later, Please
summary: Move slow work out of the request with a message queue — and learn the acks, retries and dead letters that keep jobs from vanishing.

goals.text: Decouple slow work with producers, a queue and consumers
Use the backlog as a buffer and scale consumers
Make consumers idempotent and park poison jobs

steps.title: The upload that takes eight seconds
body: Snapfolio turns your photos into printed albums. Upload 40 photos and the API does everything on the spot: resize, colour-correct, lay out pages, render a print-ready PDF — then replies.
On a quiet Tuesday that's 8 seconds of spinner. Annoying, but it works.

card.title: Inside one upload request
lines: receive 40 photos
resize · colour-correct · lay out pages
render print PDF
= reply after 8.2 s

steps.title: Everyone uploads after the weekend
body: Sunday evening, uploads triple. Each one holds an API thread for 8 seconds of CPU work, so the thread pool fills, new uploads queue inside the server, and the load balancer's 30-second timeout starts cutting them off.
The user sees an error after half a minute, and the half-finished album is simply gone.

callout.text: Doing slow work inside a request ties your response time — and your failure rate — to the slowest thing you do.

card.title: Sunday evening
lines: ! the rest time out and are lost

steps.title: Take a ticket
body: Split the work. The API — now a producer — checks the upload, stores the photos and puts a small job message on a message queue, then answers 202 Accepted with a job id. Separate consumer processes, the workers, pull jobs and do the rendering.
The app shows “We're building your album” and notifies the user when it's ready. Users wait for a reply that is honest instead of one that is slow.

card.title: Accept now, work later
lines: API: validate, store photos, enqueue job
reply 202 Accepted + job id
worker: pull job, render, save
= upload answers in 160 ms

steps.title: The backlog absorbs the spike
body: Sunday again. Jobs now arrive three times faster than two workers can finish them, so the backlog grows. That's fine: the queue stores jobs durably, the API still answers in 160 ms, and nothing is dropped.
The cost moved from “errors now” to “albums ready later”. Watch the age of the oldest job — that's the delay your users actually feel.

card.title: The queue is a shock absorber
lines: # the backlog grows, but nothing is lost
# users still get an instant reply

steps.title: More hands on the line
body: Because producers and consumers only share the queue, each side scales on its own. Add workers and they simply start pulling jobs too; no load balancer or API change is needed.
Autoscaling on queue depth (or oldest-job age) adds workers on Sunday and removes them on Tuesday, so you pay for rendering only when there's rendering to do.

card.title: Scale the consumers, not the API
lines: 1 worker ≈ 15 albums / min
6 workers ≈ 90 / min = the Sunday peak
# autoscale on queue depth or oldest-job age
= backlog 4,800 → 300 in 40 min

steps.title: Taken is not the same as done
body: Worker W3 runs out of memory on a huge panorama and crashes. Our queue was configured to delete a job the moment a worker receives it, so W3's 12 in-progress jobs vanish with it.
Twelve customers paid for albums that will never arrive, and no error was logged anywhere.

card.title: W3 crashed mid-render
lines: queue removed its jobs when W3 took them
W3 held 12 jobs in memory
! 12 albums will never print

steps.title: Delete only after an acknowledgement
body: With acknowledgements, receiving a job just hides it for a visibility timeout. The worker deletes it by sending an ack after the PDF is safely saved. If the worker dies first, the timeout expires and the job reappears for another worker.
This gives at-least-once delivery: every job is processed, possibly more than once.

callout.text: Set the visibility timeout comfortably above the slowest normal job, or long jobs get handed out twice while still running.

changes: ~ Jobs hidden on receive, deleted on ack

card.title: Acknowledge, then forget
lines: worker takes job → job hidden, not deleted
finish → worker sends ack → job deleted
no ack within 5 min → job visible again
= W3's 12 jobs go to other workers

steps.title: Twice is the price of never zero
body: At-least-once has a catch: a worker can finish the work and crash just before its ack. The job comes back and another worker renders the same album again.

So consumers must be idempotent: running a job twice has the same effect as once. Write output to a path derived from the job id, record “job 9187 done” in the same transaction as the result, and skip jobs already marked done.

callout.text: “Exactly once” delivery is not something a network can promise. You build effectively once from at-least-once plus idempotent processing.

card.title: Same job, twice
lines: W3 saved album 9187, then crashed before ack
job reappears → W4 renders it again
naive: print + ship 2 books, bill twice
= idempotent: 'job 9187 done' → skip

steps.title: The job that always fails
body: One album contains a corrupt TIFF that crashes the renderer every time. Redelivery makes it a poison message: it bounces from worker to worker forever, burning capacity.
Cap the attempts. Retry with growing delays, and after the 5th failure move the job to a dead-letter queue (DLQ). Alert on DLQ size; someone inspects, fixes and replays those jobs later.

card.title: A poison message
lines: crashes every worker that tries it
retry with backoff: 10 s, 40 s, 3 min…
after 5 attempts → dead-letter queue
= the line keeps moving; a human looks later

steps.title: A queue is not infinite
body: A queue hides a mismatch, it doesn't fix it. If jobs arrive faster than you can ever process them, the backlog grows without end, delays reach days and eventually storage runs out.

Backpressure means telling producers to slow down: bound the queue, and when it's full make the API answer 503 with “try again later” (or throttle uploads), while autoscaling catches up. Better a clear “not now” than a promise you can't keep.

card.title: If in > out, forever
lines: # bound the queue · alert on oldest-job age
# push back on producers or add consumers

steps.title: Fast replies, durable work
body:
• Queue slow work: reply fast with a job id, let consumers do the rest.
  • The backlog buffers spikes; scale consumers on its depth and age.
  • Ack after the work is done → at-least-once delivery.
  • At-least-once needs idempotent consumers.
  • Cap retries and park poison jobs in a dead-letter queue.
  • Bound queues and push back when consumers can't keep up.
